Yes. The most directly relevant paper argues that chaotic dynamics make standard RL hard because sensitivity to initial conditions creates high-variance bootstrap targets and poorly conditioned gradients, while distributional RL helps because the return distribution evolves more regularly than individual trajectories under the 1-Wasserstein metric, giving a smoother Bellman objective and better conditioned learning in chaotic systems [1].

A different but related distributional RL result does not focus on chaos directly: it studies how return-distribution learning dynamics reveal a dynamic-programming-like propagation structure and uses that to guide sampling in StructRL [2]. Other supplied papers discuss chaos with generative forecasting or deep learning objectives rather than RL, so they are relevant to chaotic dynamics but not specifically to distributional RL [3, 5, 8, 9].
